strengths: Important and timely research question: The paper rigorously investigates whether modern video generative models act as genuine physical world models or merely generate visually plausible textures.

Principled evaluation framework: Instead of relying on subjective human/VLM evaluations (which are prone to hallucinations) or rigid ground-truth trajectory matching (which unfairly penalizes valid alternate trajectories due to unobserved parameters), Morpheus evaluates adherence to governing equations of motion via Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and conservation of physical invariants.

Well-grounded physical dataset: The benchmark builds upon 130 carefully recorded real-world laboratory experiments across nine classical Newtonian mechanics setups (e.g., pendulums, projectile motion, collisions, rolling, sliding), complemented by realistic video-to-video style transfers to enhance visual diversity.

Comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art models: Evaluates multiple prominent open-source video models (WAN-2.1, COSMOS, CogVideoX, LTX-Video, PyramidalFlow) across varied conditioning schemes (single-frame, multi-frame, keyframe) and prompt complexities.

Detailed transparency and diagnostic pipeline: Includes automated quality discard filters (tracking permanence, duplicates, stillness) and provides extensive derivations and ablations in the appendix.
weaknesses: Scale and physical diversity: The underlying testbed consists of 130 real videos across 9 mechanical setups, all restricted to 2D planar motion orthogonal to a static camera under simplified assumptions (e.g., negligible air resistance, frictionless or simple damping). While augmented, the diversity of physical phenomena remains limited.

Sensitivity in scoring heuristics: As acknowledged in Appendix D.5, the Physical Invariance score is sensitive to the sliding window length. Choosing the maximum score across sliding windows could risk overestimating plausibility on short stable segments. Additionally, using different window ratios for real (L/10) versus generated (L/4) videos slightly confounds direct metric comparisons.

Reliance on 2D vision backbones: Extraction of trajectories relies on SAM 2, DEVA, and Depth Anything V2. Tracking noise and perspective/uncalibrated pixel-to-metric conversions can introduce artifacts into velocity and acceleration estimates despite filtering and smoothing.

Omission of leading closed-source models: While budget constraints are noted, the lack of full evaluation on state-of-the-art closed-source models (such as Sora, Veo 2/3, Kling, or Gen-3) leaves open the question of whether scaling closed foundation models bridges the physical reasoning gap observed here.

strengths: Principled Evaluation Beyond Trajectory Matching: Unlike prior benchmarks that rely on naive pixel-level trajectory matching (which suffers from false negatives due to unobservable initial velocities or friction) or subjective VLM prompting, Morpheus assesses generated videos via governing differential equations (using PINNs) and invariant conservation laws (energy, momentum, period).

High-Quality Real-World Controlled Dataset: The collection of 130 laboratory-controlled physical experiments covering 9 fundamental Newtonian systems (free fall, projectile motion, rolling, sliding, pendulums, collisions, springs) provides a grounded physical baseline, with real-world videos achieving near-perfect scores (0.85–0.99) validating the evaluation framework.

Extensive and Timely Empirical Study: The benchmark tests a comprehensive suite of modern video generative models (including COSMOS, WAN2.1, CogVideoX, LTX, PyramidalFlow) over 9,000 generated videos across diverse conditioning paradigms (single-frame, multi-frame, keyframe interpolation) and prompt augmentations.

Informative Diagnostic Taxonomy: Decomposing evaluation into structural failure modes (discard rate: disappearance, duplication, stillness) alongside fine-grained physical adherence (dynamical and invariance scores) provides clear diagnostic insights into where current video generation models fail as physical world models.

Transparent Limitations Discussion: The authors candidly discuss key assumptions and boundaries in Section 6 and Appendix E, including static camera constraints, 2D-to-3D projection ambiguities, and neglect of unmodeled dissipative forces.
weaknesses: Trajectory Extraction and Tracking Sensitivity: The evaluation heavily relies on 2D tracking pipelines (SAM-2, Grounded-DINO, central differencing, Savitzky-Golay smoothing). Tracking noise or bounding-box jitter can disproportionately amplify higher-order derivatives (velocity and acceleration), potentially penalizing visually plausible videos due to tracking artifacts rather than generative failures.

Window Selection Heuristics: The Physical Invariance score evaluates trajectories by selecting the highest-scoring sliding time window (spanning only 10%–25% of the clip duration) to avoid boundary fluctuations. This heuristic risks masking non-physical behavior or trajectory drift outside the optimal window.

Simplifying Assumptions in Physical Models: Several experiments assume idealized, frictionless, or undamped conditions (e.g., ignoring air drag, rolling resistance, or rotational kinetic energy in collisions). While necessary for closed-form invariants, generated videos that realistically exhibit subtle damping or drag could be unfairly scored lower against idealized equations.

Computational Overhead of PINN Fitting: Fitting a PINN per trajectory for 200,000 iterations poses non-trivial computational overhead for large-scale evaluation, and the sensitivity of the Dynamical score to the physics loss weight (lambda) is not fully ablated.

Minor Presentation and Typographical Errors: The manuscript contains noticeable typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'extarct' on page 6, 'correspoding' on page 6, 'comparsion' on page 2, and 'Reproducability' on page 35) that should be corrected in the final revision.

strengths: Important and timely research question: addresses whether state-of-the-art video generative models function as authentic physical world models or merely surface-level perceptual simulators.

Principled evaluation paradigm: moves beyond subjective human/VLM evaluations and brittle trajectory-matching by assessing adherence to fundamental physical conservation laws (e.g., energy, momentum, period) and equations of motion, which do not falsely penalize valid alternate initial velocities or hidden factors.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: evaluates multiple leading open-source video models (COSMOS, WAN-2.1, CogVideoX, LTX-Video, PyramidalFlow) across different conditioning paradigms (single-frame, multi-frame, keyframe) across over 9,000 generated video sequences.
Thorough error taxonomy and discard analysis: explicitly decomposes common generative failures into stillness, duplication, and disappearance before computing fine-grained physical dynamics metrics.
Honest discussion of experimental limitations, including assumptions of negligible friction/air resistance and static camera constraints.
weaknesses: Unclear metric calibration between pixel coordinates and real-world physical units: In Section 4.2 and Appendix D.5, calculating total energy conservation ($E/m = 0.5(v_x^2 + v_y^2) + gy$) requires converting 2D pixel velocities and positions into metric units so that the kinetic and potential energy terms scale commensurately with $g$. The manuscript mentions that proper coordinate scaling is essential, but does not clearly explain how the pixel-to-meter scale factor is reliably recovered for generated videos where camera intrinsics/extrinsics and depth are uncalibrated.

Methodological justification for PINN fitting over direct ODE residual evaluation: In Section 4.1, training an independent PINN for 200,000 iterations per video trajectory to calculate the Dynamical Score via NMSE introduces significant computational overhead and hyperparameter sensitivity ($\lambda=1$). The authors do not adequately justify why fitting a neural network regressor is preferable to directly computing numerical ODE residuals on the smoothed trajectory.

Selection bias in Physical Score windowing: Section D.5 specifies that scores are calculated using a sliding window and the maximum score across all segments is chosen as the trajectory's overall score. Selecting the best sub-window (especially using different window ratios: 10% for real videos vs. 25% for generated videos) risks rewarding trajectories that are completely non-physical for the majority of the sequence as long as a single short window appears smooth or static.

Relatively small base dataset: The benchmark is built on 130 recorded real-world videos across 9 experiment types (some having as few as 7 to 10 recordings). While style transfer augmentation increases appearance diversity, the underlying physical trajectory variations remain limited.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: moving beyond pixel-level trajectory matching (which wrongly penalizes alternative physically valid realizations due to unobserved initial conditions) and VLM judges (which hallucinate physical violations on real-world ground-truth data).

Principled and well-formulated physics-informed methodology: incorporating both continuous equations of motion via Physics-Informed Neural Networks (Dynamical score) and conservation of fundamental physical quantities (Physical Invariance score).

High-quality, controlled benchmark: curated dataset comprising 130 real-world recordings across 9 fundamental Newtonian mechanics setups (falling, projectile, collisions, single/double pendulums, etc.) alongside visually augmented variants using mask-guided style transfer.

Comprehensive empirical study evaluating modern state-of-the-art closed-source (Veo3, Kling) and open-source (Wan2.1, COSMOS, CogVideoX, PyramidalFlow, LTX) models under diverse conditioning regimes (single-frame, multi-frame, keyframe interpolation).

Extensive validation and ablations: demonstration of real-vs-real trajectory matching failure vs. Morpheus consistency, strong correlation with human judgment on motion plausibility (Spearman rho = 0.708), depth-consistency verification, PINN architecture sweeps, and tracking noise/gap robustness tests.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to planar 2D trajectories recorded from a static orthogonal camera view; while this is an effective choice for eliminating camera-motion confounders, it limits applicability to complex 3D embodied interactions and uncalibrated dynamic-camera settings.

The Physical Invariance score is computed on the 'best-scoring 25% sliding window' to avoid impact-boundary fluctuations; while the 100% window ablation in Table 8 shows preserved relative rankings, evaluating solely the best window risks masking severe non-physical behavior occurring elsewhere in the clip.

Physical parameter ambiguity: properties such as precise mass, spring stiffness, and exact surface friction cannot be fully conveyed through visual prompts, meaning the metric necessarily assumes idealized Newtonian conditions (e.g., zero air drag), which could mildly penalize realistic dissipative dynamics.

strengths: Compelling and rigorous conceptual framing: The paper clearly identifies and empirically proves the failure modes of existing evaluation paradigms (e.g., the ambiguity and excessive rigidity of direct trajectory matching shown via real-vs-real comparisons, and the unreliability/hallucinations of VLM-based judges shown with VideoPHY-2).

Principled physics-informed methodology: Formulating plausibility checks through governing ODE fitting with PINNs (Dynamical score) and conservation laws (Physical Invariance score) allows evaluation without requiring full ground-truth parameter observability (e.g., unknown exact mass or friction).

Grounded in real-world experiments: Curating 130 controlled physical experiments across 9 diverse Newtonian mechanical systems (pendulums, collisions, projectiles, rolling, sliding, etc.), coupled with style-transfer augmentations, provides a reliable and realistic testbed.

Comprehensive empirical study: Evaluating leading proprietary (Veo3, Kling-2.5) and open-source models (Wan2.1, COSMOS, CogVideoX, LTX) across single-frame, multi-frame, and keyframe conditioning yields valuable insights into where and why video models fail to simulate physical dynamics.

Thorough validation and robustness analyses: Includes scale-invariance checks, depth consistency verification via Depth Anything V2/V3, tracking noise/gap perturbation experiments, PINN architecture sweeps, and human alignment studies.
weaknesses: Restricted physical scope: The framework is strictly confined to 2D planar, rigid-body Newtonian dynamics with static orthogonal camera views. While well-justified for controlled measurement, it does not yet extend to 3D out-of-plane motions, deformable bodies, or fluid dynamics.

Heuristic sliding-window selection for invariance scoring: Selecting the best-scoring 25% window to avoid impact/boundary noise, while ablated in Appendix D.9, risks overlooking transient unphysical artifacts outside the chosen segment.

Moderate dataset volume: While each experiment features multiple trials and controlled parameter variations, 130 base physical recording setups remain modest compared to large-scale video benchmarks, though augmented tenfold via video-to-video transfer.

Reliance on zero-shot perception pipelines: Centroid extraction depends on SAM-2 segmentation and heuristic discard filtering; although the discard filter is verified against human majority voting, it exhibits a notable false-negative rate (16.9%) where invalid generations pass to the scoring stage.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental, timely question in generative modeling: evaluating whether contemporary video generative models (VGMs) respect true Newtonian physical laws rather than merely generating visually plausible or perceptually convincing motion.

Methodologically sound formulation that moves beyond both subjective/hallucinatory VLM judges and overly rigid trajectory-matching metrics by utilizing Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and conservation of physical invariants (e.g., energy, momentum, period).

Thorough benchmark validation: the authors demonstrate that real-world videos achieve near-ceiling scores (Dynamical > 0.96, Invariance >= 0.90), show why trajectory matching fails on real-vs-real pairs (IoU < 0.05), and prove that state-of-the-art VLM evaluators hallucinate violations on clean ground-truth physical recordings.

Comprehensive experimental execution covering nine competitive open- and closed-source models (including Wan2.1, Veo3, Kling-2.5, and Cosmos), alongside rigorous ablations on prompt upsampling, temporal conditioning (single-frame vs. multi-frame vs. keyframe), PINN architectures, trajectory noise, and human judgment correlation (Spearman rho = 0.708).
weaknesses: The physical scope is constrained to 2D planar rigid-body Newtonian mechanics recorded with a static orthogonal camera; while well-justified for clean trajectory extraction, it leaves out 3D dynamics, deformable objects, fluids, and non-planar interactions.

Heuristics in score aggregation: evaluating the Physical Invariance score on the best-scoring 25% sliding window (to bypass tracking spikes during impact) risks ignoring localized physical violations elsewhere in the clip, even though Appendix D.9 shows relative model rankings remain stable under full-trajectory scoring.
The dataset size of 130 raw experimental recordings across nine archetypes is relatively compact, although expanded via video style transfer augmentations.
